segments: The Seventh Period.
The Kings of the Pagan Greeks.
[he lived, in a tub] and not in a house.
And someone said to him:
"If the tub is broken, what will you do?" And he replied:
"If the tub is broken,
the place where the tub is will not be broken."
For he used to say that the outward beauty of the body indicates the inward beauty of the soul.
And when the Athenians saw that he chose handsome youths to teach,
they supposed concerning him that he was a lover of boys.
And because he greatly rebuked and censured the king for his licentiousness,
he instructed his sons Anytus and Meletus, and they accused him of sodomy;
and thus he killed him with poison.
For this is mentioned by the holy Gregory the Theologian in the second of the Invectives, when he says:
"The love of beauty of Socrates—
for I blush," he says,
"at the love of boys—
even if it is cloaked in praises."
After the Persian Darius, Alexander reigned in Hellas at the age of twenty years.
And he was three cubits tall.
And he became far greater than all the kings who were before him.
And he subdued many countries,
and destroyed thirty-five kings.
And his army consisted of one hundred and twenty thousand.
And in the sixth year of Darius, which was also that of Alexander, they drew up for battle in Issus, a city in Cilicia.
And Alexander conquered,
and Darius was killed,
and the kingdom of the Persians came to an end.
And here begins the seventh period,
which passes from the kings of the Persians to the kings of the pagan Greeks. Alexander survived Darius by six years,
after he had killed Darius and the prophecy of Daniel was fulfilled,
concerning the he-goat of the goats which came and killed the ram.
